title: Observation framework (@Observable)
summary: `@Observable` (iOS 17+) makes a class trackable property by property. A view only refreshes when a property it actually read changes - fewer useless redraws than `ObservableObject`.
body: **In simple words:** Put `@Observable` on a class. While SwiftUI runs a view's `body`, it notes which properties you read. Later, if one of those properties changes, only that view refreshes. Changing a property nobody displayed does nothing.

**Compared to `ObservableObject`:** there, any `@Published` change told every observing view "something changed", even if that view did not use the property. With many views on one model, this caused a lot of wasted work.

**How it works under the hood:** the macro turns each stored property into a computed one that reports reads ("access") and writes ("withMutation") to an `ObservationRegistrar`. `withObservationTracking` records reads and calls back on the first change.

**Useful details:** `@ObservationIgnored` for properties that should not trigger updates (caches, task handles). Works with optionals, arrays of models and nested models. Mutate UI models on the main actor.
**Outside SwiftUI (Swift 6.2):** `Observations { model.value }` gives an async sequence of changes.
keyPoints: Tracking is per property and per view, based on what `body` actually read.
Replaces `ObservableObject` + `@Published` with less boilerplate and fewer redraws.
Use `@State` to own, plain property to read, `@Bindable` for bindings, `.environment` to inject.

code.caption: Only the view that reads `progress` redraws

mistakes: Reading a fast-changing property in a large parent view, causing the whole screen to redraw - move it to a small child.
followups: **How do you migrate from ObservableObject?** Replace with `@Observable`, remove `@Published`, `@StateObject` → `@State`, `@ObservedObject` → plain property/`@Bindable`, `@EnvironmentObject` → `@Environment(Type.self)`.
